Cruciform means "shaped like a cross." If something is cruciform, its overall shape or layout resembles a cross — two straight elements (bars, corridors, beams, wings, arms, etc.) crossing each other at right angles (90°), creating four sections that extend outward from a central point.
Exactly what "cross" shape does it mean?

The cross that cruciform refers to can be either of these two forms:

A Greek cross — all four arms are exactly equal in length. Think of the plus sign (+). This is the more geometrically balanced version.

A Latin cross — one arm (almost always the bottom one) is longer than the other three. Think of the traditional Christian cross (†). This is the more widely recognized version in everyday culture.

Both shapes are correctly called cruciform. The defining feature in either case is the four outward-extending arms and the right-angle intersection at the center.

Cruciform is a formal, precise word used across many different fields. Here's where you'll most commonly encounter it:

Architecture — This is the most frequent use. Many traditional Christian churches, when viewed from directly above (a bird's-eye view), are built in a cruciform shape. The long central hall (called the nave) and the shorter hall crossing it (called the transept) together form a cross. Famous examples include St. Peter's Basilica in Rome and Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. Architects also design cruciform floor plans for other buildings — hospitals, palaces, libraries — when they want to maximize the number of wings branching off a central core.

Anatomy and medicine — The body contains several structures described as cruciform. The most important are the cruciform ligaments — tough bands of connective tissue in your knee that cross each other diagonally (forming an X rather than a +). Doctors also describe certain surgical incisions, muscle arrangements, or anatomical features as cruciform when they form a cross-shaped pattern.

Aviation and military technology — Many aircraft, rockets, and missiles have cruciform tails or cruciform fins — four stabilizing surfaces arranged in a cross pattern around the rear of the vehicle. When you look at the back of the vehicle head-on, you'd see a plus sign shape. This arrangement provides balanced stability in all directions.

Botany (plant science) — A large family of flowering plants — including cabbage, mustard, broccoli, and radishes — are known for having four petals arranged in a cross shape. These flowers are described as cruciform, and the whole plant family is sometimes called the "crucifers" for this reason.

Molecular biology — DNA molecules can sometimes fold into cruciform structures — a cross-shaped configuration — especially in certain genetic sequences. Scientists use the term cruciform DNA to describe this shape.

Religious and decorative art — A halo depicted as a cross (rather than a plain ring) is called a cruciform halo. It appears frequently in Christian paintings and mosaics, typically around the head of Jesus or God. Cruciform shapes also appear in jewelry, medals, architectural ornamentation, and military decorations.
How it behaves in a sentence

Cruciform always describes a noun — it answers the question "what shape does this thing have?" You'll typically see it placed directly before the noun it describes, or after a linking verb like "is" or "was":

  • "The cathedral has a cruciform layout."
  • "The aircraft's tail was cruciform."
  • "They built the hospital in a cruciform arrangement."
  • "The ligament follows a cruciform pattern."

Cruciform refers to overall shape or arrangement — not to the material, the size, or the purpose. A tiny DNA molecule, a massive cathedral, and a rocket fin can all be cruciform, because the word only speaks to form. It also carries a slightly formal or technical register, so you'd see it in architectural writing, medical texts, scientific papers, and art history — rather than in everyday casual conversation, where someone would simply say "cross-shaped" instead. Cruciform is just the single, precise word that says the same thing more elegantly and concisely.
